title: Phishing Awareness & Email Defense
summary: Learn how to spot deceptive emails, malicious attachments, domain spoofing, and urgent credential harvesting requests.
what_is_it: Phishing is a social engineering technique where attackers impersonate trustworthy entities (banks, IT support, executives) to trick individuals into disclosing passwords, downloading malware, or authorizing unauthorized wire transfers.
why_it_matters: Over 80% of reported security incidents begin with a phishing lure. A single compromised credential can lead to enterprise-wide ransomware or data breach.
warning_signs: Urgent or threatening language (e.g., 'Account suspended within 2 hours')
Mismatched sender display names and actual email headers/domains
Generic greetings like 'Dear Customer' when personal context is expected
Unexpected invoices, shipping notifications, or password reset confirmations
Embedded links pointing to unfamiliar or look-alike domains
safe_practices: Hover over links to inspect the destination URL before clicking
Verify unexpected requests directly through a known, trusted out-of-band channel
Never enter corporate credentials on external or unfamiliar websites
Use email client phishing reporting buttons immediately upon discovery
what_to_do: If you clicked a suspicious link or provided credentials, immediately disconnect from network, change your password from an isolated trusted device, and alert your SOC/IT Security team.

title: Password Security & Passphrase Hygiene
summary: Master strong password generation, password manager usage, and avoidance of credential reuse across accounts.
what_is_it: Password hygiene involves creating complex, unique passwords or multi-word passphrases for every single service to prevent credential stuffing and brute-force attacks.
why_it_matters: Attackers leverage massive leaked credential databases. If you reuse the same password on multiple sites, a breach at one vendor immediately exposes your enterprise and personal accounts.
warning_signs: Prompts to reuse familiar passwords across personal and work services
Using easily guessable personal info (birthdays, pet names, company name)
Storing passwords in unencrypted text files, spreadsheets, or sticky notes
safe_practices: Use passphrases consisting of 4+ random words (e.g., 'correct-horse-battery-staple')
Utilize an approved enterprise password manager to generate and store random 16+ character passwords
Never share passwords over email, chat, or voice communications
what_to_do: If you suspect a password has been compromised or leaked, reset it immediately and enable multi-factor authentication across all associated services.

title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) & Phishing Resistance
summary: Understand MFA mechanisms, authenticator apps, hardware security keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn), and MFA prompt fatigue attacks.
what_is_it: Multi-Factor Authentication requires two or more distinct verification factors (something you know, something you have, something you are) before granting access.
why_it_matters: MFA blocks over 99% of automated credential stuffing attacks. However, modern adversaries use push-fatigue or adversary-in-the-middle phishing to bypass basic SMS/push methods.
warning_signs: Receiving unsolicited MFA push notifications when you are not actively logging in
Phone calls from individuals claiming to be 'IT Support' asking you to read a one-time passcode
safe_practices: Prefer authenticator apps (TOTP) or hardware security keys (FIDO2/Passkeys) over SMS
Always reject unrequested MFA push notifications and report them immediately
Use number matching on push notifications to ensure prompt origin alignment
what_to_do: If you receive repetitive unexpected MFA prompts, click 'Deny', report the incident to your SOC as a suspected MFA fatigue attack, and change your primary password.

title: Social Engineering & Vishing/Smishing Defense
summary: Recognize psychological manipulation techniques including phone pretexting (vishing), SMS scams (smishing), and impersonation.
what_is_it: Social engineering exploits human psychology (trust, fear, urgency, curiosity, or helpfulness) rather than technical software bugs to manipulate people into breaking security procedures.
why_it_matters: Adversaries research public LinkedIn profiles, organizational charts, and vendor relationships to craft highly credible impersonation scenarios.
warning_signs: Callers claiming to be executive leadership demanding emergency exceptions to financial or data release protocols
SMS text messages demanding urgent parcel fee payment or urgent payroll updates
Pressure to bypass standard security verifications or authorization flows
safe_practices: Always verify caller identities via corporate directory call-backs before sharing sensitive data
Follow dual-custody authorization policies for all wire transfers and access grants
Maintain a healthy culture of verification: asking for confirmation is good security, not rudeness
what_to_do: Hang up or cease communication, document the caller's claimed identity and request details, and inform your security team.

title: Safe Web Browsing & Malicious Downloads
summary: Navigate the web securely, detect typosquatting domains, avoid drive-by downloads, and manage browser extensions.
what_is_it: Safe browsing encompasses habits and browser settings that minimize exposure to web exploits, malicious redirects, compromised advertising networks, and fake download portals.
why_it_matters: Compromised benign websites and malvertising campaigns can silently redirect users to exploit kits or trick them into installing backdoor-laden software packages.
warning_signs: Browser warnings indicating expired or invalid TLS/SSL certificates
Unexpected prompts to download executable files (.exe, .scr, .iso, .vbs) when visiting general web pages
Aggressive popups claiming your computer is infected with viruses with a phone number to call
safe_practices: Only download software from official vendor repositories and approved corporate catalogs
Audit browser extensions periodically and remove unneeded or suspicious add-ons
Ensure HTTPS encryption is active on all web sites where information is submitted
what_to_do: If a webpage triggers an unexpected file download, do NOT open the file. Delete it from your downloads directory and notify IT security.

title: Secure Wi-Fi & Public Network Protection
summary: Safeguard communications on hotel, airport, and coffee shop networks using enterprise VPNs and encrypted protocols.
what_is_it: Public Wi-Fi networks are often unencrypted or shared with unknown users, enabling attackers to perform eavesdropping, evil twin attacks, and man-in-the-middle credential interception.
why_it_matters: Connecting to rogue access points allows adversaries to inspect unencrypted traffic, inject malicious code into cleartext streams, or spoof DNS resolutions.
warning_signs: Wi-Fi networks with generic names matching public locations but lacking password authentication
Certificate warning banners popping up on reputable websites after connecting to public Wi-Fi
Automated connection to open networks without explicit user approval
safe_practices: Always connect through an enterprise VPN before accessing internal applications on public networks
Disable 'Auto-Connect to Open Wi-Fi' on laptops and mobile devices
Use cellular hotspot tethering as a secure alternative to untrusted public networks
what_to_do: Immediately disconnect from suspicious public networks, verify VPN tunnel status, and inspect your active browser sessions for certificate warnings.

title: Software Patching & Vulnerability Hygiene
summary: Understand the critical role of timely operating system, browser, and third-party software updates in closing known security holes.
what_is_it: Software patching is the systematic deployment of vendor-released security fixes to remediate vulnerabilities (CVEs) before threat actors can exploit them.
why_it_matters: The majority of successful ransomware and cyber intrusions exploit known vulnerabilities for which patches were available months prior.
warning_signs: Postponing reboot or update prompts repeatedly for weeks
Running deprecated software versions that have reached End-of-Life (EOL)
safe_practices: Enable automatic updates for operating systems, web browsers, and productivity tools
Restart devices promptly when update notifications require a reboot
Report legacy, unpatchable systems to IT for compensating network isolation
what_to_do: Check your system update settings weekly to ensure all critical security patches are installed and verified.

title: Ransomware Awareness & Defensive Measures
summary: Understand how ransomware propagates, the importance of offline backups, and early detection indicators.
what_is_it: Ransomware is malicious software designed to deny access to computer systems or data through encryption, often coupled with data exfiltration extortion.
why_it_matters: Ransomware attacks can paralyze entire hospitals, municipal services, universities, and enterprise supply chains, causing millions in losses and operational downtime.
warning_signs: Sudden disk activity accompanied by files changing extensions to unknown formats
Text or HTML ransom notes appearing on desktops or network file shares
Endpoint protection alerts flagging unauthorized volume shadow copy deletion
safe_practices: Maintain immutable, disconnected (3-2-1 rule) backups of all critical data
Apply strict least privilege access controls to network shares and folders
Never enable macros on untrusted Office documents received via email
what_to_do: Immediately isolate the infected device from Wi-Fi and wired Ethernet to stop lateral propagation, do NOT reboot (to preserve RAM forensics), and notify incident response.

title: Removable Media & USB Security
summary: Mitigate risks associated with rogue USB drives, BadUSB firmware payloads, and data exfiltration through external drives.
what_is_it: Removable media safety involves secure handling of USB flash drives, external hard drives, and SD cards to prevent automated payload execution and data leakage.
why_it_matters: Attackers deliberately drop malicious USB drives in parking lots or lobbies ('USB baiting') programmed as HID keyboard emulators that inject commands within seconds.
warning_signs: Finding unattended USB drives labeled with enticing titles (e.g., 'Executive Payroll 2026', 'Confidential Bonuses')
Unexpected keyboard or terminal keystroke bursts upon inserting a USB device
safe_practices: Never insert found, unverified, or gift promotional USB drives into corporate systems
Use hardware write-blocking or IT-managed encrypted storage for authorized transfers
Turn off AutoRun and AutoPlay capabilities across all operating systems
what_to_do: Hand in any found USB drives directly to the security operations center or IT help desk without plugging them in.

title: Data Privacy & Information Classification
summary: Handle sensitive data (PII, PHI, financial records, IP) appropriately according to data classification standards.
what_is_it: Data privacy practices ensure confidential and personal information is stored, processed, shared, and disposed of in compliance with regulatory and organizational policies.
why_it_matters: Data breaches result in substantial regulatory penalties (GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA), reputational damage, and loss of customer trust.
warning_signs: Storing customer PII or credit card numbers in publicly accessible cloud buckets
Sending unencrypted confidential spreadsheets over standard external email
Disposing of paper documents containing personal data without shredding
safe_practices: Classify files (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) and apply appropriate encryption
Utilize enterprise data loss prevention (DLP) tools and secure file transfer mechanisms
Regularly review shared folder permissions and revoke external access when no longer required
what_to_do: If you inadvertently share confidential data with an unauthorized party, alert your privacy officer and security team immediately for containment.

title: Mobile Device Security & App Permissions
summary: Protect smartphones and tablets against mobile malware, excessive app permissions, and unauthorized device access.
what_is_it: Mobile security includes securing mobile operating systems, isolating corporate data (MDM/MAM), and monitoring application permissions.
why_it_matters: Smartphones hold corporate emails, 2FA authenticator apps, sensitive messages, and location history, making them prime targets for threat actors.
warning_signs: Apps requesting unnecessary permissions (e.g., flashlight app requesting contacts and SMS access)
Unusual battery drain, excessive data usage, or device overheating when idle
Prompts to install configuration profiles or certificates from untrusted web pages
safe_practices: Enforce strong device passcodes, biometric locks, and automatic screen timeouts
Only install apps from official app stores (Google Play, Apple App Store)
Keep mobile OS and apps updated to latest supported releases
what_to_do: If a mobile device is lost, stolen, or compromised, initiate remote wipe procedures via your company MDM portal or mobile vendor cloud portal.

title: Remote Work & Home Network Defense
summary: Implement defensive measures for hybrid work environments, home router security, and physical workstation privacy.
what_is_it: Remote work security establishes enterprise-grade safeguards for home offices and traveling employees outside traditional perimeter firewalls.
why_it_matters: Home routers with default credentials and unpatched IoT devices on home networks can serve as stepping stones to breach work laptops.
warning_signs: Default admin passwords unchanged on home Wi-Fi routers
Family members or guests using corporate workstations for browsing or gaming
Working in public spaces where screens are visible to bystanders (shoulder surfing)
safe_practices: Change default router credentials and enable WPA3/WPA2-AES encryption with strong keys
Keep work devices dedicated solely to corporate business tasks
Use privacy screen filters when working in transit or coffee shops
what_to_do: Segment home IoT devices into an isolated guest network so corporate laptops remain separated from smart TVs and IoT appliances.

title: Cloud Account Security & API Token Hygiene
summary: Secure cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP, SaaS) through least privilege, token rotation, and activity monitoring.
what_is_it: Cloud account security encompasses identity management, IAM role scoping, session management, and protecting API keys and credentials.
why_it_matters: Leaked API keys committed to public GitHub repositories or over-privileged IAM roles can give attackers complete control over cloud infrastructure in seconds.
warning_signs: Hardcoding API keys or secret tokens directly inside source code or git commits
Root / Global Admin accounts used for day-to-day administrative operations
Cloud audit logs disabled or unmonitored for anomalous geographic logins
safe_practices: Never commit secrets to source code; use environment variables and Secret Managers
Apply the Principle of Least Privilege: grant only the exact permissions needed
Rotate API keys and service tokens regularly and enforce short-lived session tokens
what_to_do: If an API key or cloud credential is leaked, immediately revoke it, audit cloud CloudTrail/audit logs for unauthorized actions, and reissue new credentials.

title: Incident Reporting & Timely Escalation
summary: Empower users to report security anomalies promptly without fear of retribution, accelerating SOC response.
what_is_it: Incident reporting is the established protocol for employees to notify security teams about suspicious activities, errors, or potential breaches.
why_it_matters: The time between initial compromise and detection (dwell time) directly dictates the severity of an incident. Fast user reporting can halt an attack before data is exfiltrated.
warning_signs: Hesitation to report accidental clicks due to fear of disciplinary action
Attempting to troubleshoot or hide compromised endpoints without alerting IT security
safe_practices: Familiarize yourself with your organization's designated security contact email and hotline
Report suspected incidents immediately — early notification is always rewarded
Provide clear details: exact time, what was clicked/seen, and any error messages
what_to_do: Use your organization's PhishAlarm / Report Incident button or call the 24/7 SOC emergency extension immediately.

title: AI-Enabled Scams & Deepfake Defense
summary: Recognize synthetic voice cloning, video deepfakes, and automated hyper-personalized generative AI phishing campaigns.
what_is_it: Adversaries utilize generative AI tools to craft grammatically flawless spearphishing emails, clone executive voices for phone fraud, and generate deepfake video feeds in virtual meetings.
why_it_matters: Traditional phishing indicators like poor grammar and broken spelling are no longer reliable indicators against AI-generated attacks.
warning_signs: Voice calls from executives sounding slightly robotic or requesting emergency financial transfers with unusual urgency
Video calls where the participant's facial lighting or lip sync appears unnatural
Highly tailored emails referencing specific recent internal meetings or vendor discussions
safe_practices: Establish pre-agreed verification passphrases or out-of-band protocols for urgent financial actions
Challenge unexpected requests by asking questions only the genuine person would know
Validate executive identity via a separate communication channel (e.g., Slack/Teams ping or direct call)
what_to_do: Pause and verify any out-of-the-ordinary urgent request before taking action, even if the voice or video resembles someone you know.
